screens.title: Event-Driven Interaction Systems
screens.subtitle: Designing decoupled, C++-based interaction contracts and broadcasts

narration.text: In this chapter we'll learn how to make game objects actually respond to your traces and input without entangling classes together. We'll introduce Unreal Engine C++ interfaces — the UInterface pattern — as a contract for any object that can be 'interacted' with. You will see how a single player function can call Interact on doors, pickups, or NPCs without knowing their concrete class. Then we'll cover event dispatchers, also called delegates, which let one object broadcast an event to many listeners and keep ownership and responsibilities separated. You'll also follow a small, practical workflow: create the interface, implement it on an ADoor actor, update AMyCharacter to store a TScriptInterface pointer from a trace, and wire an InteractInput that calls Execute_Interact. Along the way we discuss BlueprintNativeEvent and why Execute_ calls are safe across Blueprint and C++. By the end you will understand when to prefer direct calls, interfaces, or dispatchers, and how to avoid common mistakes like missing bindings or dangling listeners. Think about a door in your game: you want many different systems to react when it opens. How should those systems connect so they remain modular and testable?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use UInterface for polymorphic interactions and dynamic multicast delegates for one-to-many decoupled events.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build and why they matter

narration.text: In this lesson you will design and implement a C++ interface to define an interaction contract, and you will learn why that contract improves decoupling. You will also learn to declare and use dynamic multicast delegates so actors can broadcast events to many listeners. Practically, you'll implement an Interact function that a door or pickup can implement and you will wire an OnDoorOpened dispatcher that other systems can bind to. These skills matter because they let you add new interactable types or new reactions with minimal changes elsewhere in your project. For example, adding a special sound emitter that plays when any door opens should not require editing the door class. You will practice storing a TScriptInterface on the player so traces can safely call Execute_ functions. Finally, you'll learn common pitfalls like failing to bind listeners or leaving dangling bindings when objects are destroyed. The goal is to leave you with both code patterns and an intuition for when to use an interface versus a delegate.

narration.text: This second objectives slide highlights practical milestones you'll complete while coding. First, create the InteractableInterface header and implementation with BlueprintNativeEvent signatures and compile without errors. Second, implement Interact_Implementation and CanInteract_Implementation on a simple ADoor actor so it toggles an internal state and prints a log line. Third, update AMyCharacter's trace to set a TScriptInterface pointer when an actor implements the interface, and then implement InteractInput to call Execute_CanInteract and Execute_Interact safely. Each milestone tests a specific skill: defining contracts, implementing polymorphic behavior, wiring input to interface calls, and broadcasting events to listeners. Together these milestones ensure your interaction system is flexible, testable, and integrates with both C++ and Blueprint workflows.

screens.title: UInterface: a contract, not an implementation
screens.subtitle: What UInterface gives you and how BlueprintNativeEvent fits in

narration.text: A UInterface in Unreal is a specialized C++ pattern that defines a contract of functions without prescribing class inheritance. In practice you create a UINTERFACE-derived UObject type and an IInterface C++ class containing UFUNCTION declarations. That separation lets any UObject-derived class implement the contract while keeping the interface type discoverable at runtime. The keyword BlueprintNativeEvent is crucial: it tells the engine that the function can have a default C++ implementation and still be overridden in Blueprint. Concretely, you declare void Interact(AActor* Interactor) as BlueprintNativeEvent, and implement Interact_Implementation in C++ if you want a default behavior. If a Blueprint overrides the function, the engine will call that override when using Execute_ calls. A common misconception is thinking UInterface is the same as multiple inheritance; it's not. It is a contract that classes opt into. Another is calling the interface function directly on a raw actor pointer without using Execute_. For BlueprintNativeEvent functions, Execute_FunctionName(Object, args...) ensures the call routes to the Blueprint override if one exists. Example: an ADoor can implement Interact_Implementation to toggle its state and log a message. If you rely only on class-specific casts, you'll need new casting logic for every new interactable type; interfaces remove that need. How will you structure your Interact so it stays flexible when designers want Blueprint overrides?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: UInterface defines a language-level contract; BlueprintNativeEvent lets both C++ and Blueprint provide implementations.

content.html:
Module 5 › UInterface › Definition
What a UInterface is

A UInterface provides a contract of functions that any UObject-derived class can implement, enabling polymorphic behavior without knowing concrete types.

Contract: Interact(AActor*), CanInteract(AActor*)
Specifier: BlueprintNativeEvent for C++ defaults and Blueprint overrides.
Common misconception

Interfaces are not multiple inheritance for implementation. They are a runtime contract. Calling the interface must use Execute_ for BlueprintNativeEvent routing.

Key takeaway

Design contracts, not dependencies. Use Execute_ calls to respect Blueprint overrides.

Header example (InteractableInterface.h)
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "UObject/Interface.h"
#include "InteractableInterface.generated.h"

UINTERFACE(MinimalAPI, Blueprintable)
class UInteractableInterface : public UInterface
{
	GENERATED_BODY()
};

class UNREALENGINE5CDEVELOPER_API IInteractableInterface
{
	GENERATED_BODY()

public:
	UFUNCTION(BlueprintNativeEvent, BlueprintCallable, Category = "Interaction")
	void Interact(AActor* Interactor);

	UFUNCTION(BlueprintNativeEvent, BlueprintCallable, Category = "Interaction")
	bool CanInteract(AActor* Interactor) const;
};
Example: ADoor implements Interact_Implementation to toggle bIsOpen and Broadcast OnDoorOpened.
Remember: call Execute_Interact when you have a UObject pointer to ensure Blueprint overrides run.

screens.title: Creating and implementing the interface
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step from file creation to ADoor implementation

narration.text: We'll walk through the practical steps to create an InteractableInterface and implement it on a simple ADoor class. Start by creating a new C++ class with no parent and name it InteractableInterface. Add the UINTERFACE macro and declare the IInteractableInterface class with BlueprintNativeEvent functions Interact and CanInteract. Compile to ensure your codebase recognizes the new types. Next, create an ADoor actor and include the interface header. Make ADoor inherit public IInteractableInterface in the class declaration. Implement Interact_Implementation to toggle a boolean like bIsOpen and add a UE_LOG line to confirm behavior at runtime. Implement CanInteract_Implementation to return a condition such as! bIsLocked. A likely mistake at this stage is forgetting the _Implementation suffix when defining the function in the. cpp file, which will silently keep the BlueprintNativeEvent unimplemented. Another issue is missing UPROPERTY on state variables which can affect replication and garbage collection. Test by placing ADoor instances in the level and ensuring collision blocks visibility. Finally, expose an event dispatcher in ADoor if you want other actors to react when the door opens; declare DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam and create a UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable) member, then call OnDoorOpened. Broadcast(this) inside Interact_Implementation.

keyIdea.title: Step sequence
keyIdea.text: Create interface files, implement _Implementation methods on actors, compile, test in-level placements, and optionally add a delegate to broadcast events.

content.html:
Process › Create & Implement
Implementation steps
  1. Create InteractableInterface.h/.cpp and declare BlueprintNativeEvent functions.
  2. Create ADoor actor; include header and inherit IInteractableInterface.
  3. Define Interact_Implementation(AActor* Interactor) in ADoor.cpp to toggle bIsOpen and UE_LOG a message.
  4. Implement CanInteract_Implementation to return true or a condition like !bIsLocked.
  5. Optionally: declare a delegate and broadcast OnDoorOpened.Broadcast(this) inside Interact_Implementation.
Common mistakes
Forgetting the _Implementation suffix or not compiling after adding the UINTERFACE will lead to undefined behavior or missing overrides.
ADoor snippets
// ADoor.h (excerpt)
#include "InteractableInterface.h"

UCLASS()
class ADoor : public AActor, public IInteractableInterface
{
	GENERATED_BODY()

public:
	virtual void Interact_Implementation(AActor* Interactor) override;
	virtual bool CanInteract_Implementation(AActor* Interactor) const override;
	bool bIsOpen;
};

// ADoor.cpp (excerpt)
void ADoor::Interact_Implementation(AActor* Interactor)
{
	bIsOpen = !bIsOpen;
	UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Door interacted by %s!"), *Interactor->GetName());
	// OnDoorOpened.Broadcast(this); // if declared
}

bool ADoor::CanInteract_Implementation(AActor* Interactor) const
{
	return true; // or !bIsLocked
}
Try this
Place ADoor in the level and press interact to see the log. If nothing appears, confirm collision and Trace settings from Chapter 5.1.

screens.title: Calling interface functions safely
screens.subtitle: Why and how to use Execute_ calls with BlueprintNativeEvent

narration.text: When you have a raw actor pointer from a trace, calling interface methods requires care. If the interface function is marked BlueprintNativeEvent, calling the C++ method directly on an IInterface pointer will bypass Blueprint overrides in many cases. The safe pattern is to use the generated Execute_FunctionName helper which takes a UObject pointer as the first parameter and forwards the call to either the C++ _Implementation or the Blueprint override. Practically, after your trace yields NewHitActor, check NewHitActor->Implements<UInteractableInterface>() or use Cast<IInteractableInterface>(NewHitActor). If the check succeeds, store a TScriptInterface<IInteractableInterface> on the player so you have both object and interface pointers. When the player presses Interact, call CurrentInteractableActor->Execute_CanInteract(CurrentInteractableActor. GetObject(), this) and if true call Execute_Interact similarly. A common misconception is thinking the interface pointer alone is sufficient for Execute_ calls; Execute_ expects a UObject* first. Another pitfall is calling Execute_ without validating CanInteract, which can trigger unexpected state changes. Example: if a pickup should destroy itself on interact, the Execute_Interact call may remove the object mid-frame, so plan bindings and state transitions accordingly. This pattern keeps blueprints interoperable and your game predictable across C++ and Blueprint implementations.

keyIdea.title: Safe call pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Execute_Function(ObjectPointer, args...) with TScriptInterface.GetObject() so Blueprint overrides are invoked correctly.

content.html:
Code › Execute_ call pattern
Trace → TScriptInterface → Execute
Store the actor and interface using TScriptInterface so you can call Execute_ functions safely later from input handlers.
// UpdateInteractionTrace (excerpt)
AActor* NewHitActor = nullptr;
if (bHit)
{
	NewHitActor = HitResult.GetActor();
}

if (NewHitActor && NewHitActor->Implements<UInteractableInterface>())
{
	CurrentInteractableActor.SetObject(NewHitActor);
	CurrentInteractableActor.SetInterface(Cast<IInteractableInterface>(NewHitActor));
}
else
{
	CurrentInteractableActor.SetObject(nullptr);
	CurrentInteractableActor.SetInterface(nullptr);
}

// InteractInput()
if (CurrentInteractableActor)
{
	if (CurrentInteractableActor->Execute_CanInteract(CurrentInteractableActor.GetObject(), this))
	{
		CurrentInteractableActor->Execute_Interact(CurrentInteractableActor.GetObject(), this);
	}
}
Explanation & gotchas
  • Execute_ helper requires a UObject* first argument to route to Blueprint overrides.
  • Validate CanInteract before calling Interact to avoid unintended state changes.
  • If Interact destroys the object, be careful with subsequent code that assumes the object still exists.
  • Use UPROPERTY for TScriptInterface members to participate in GC when storing UObject references.
Key takeaway
Execute_ is the safe bridge between C++ and Blueprint for interface calls.

narration.text: Event dispatchers, declared using dynamic multicast delegate macros, are the right tool when a single action should notify many listeners without hard references. In C++ you declare a delegate type like DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam(FDoorOpenedSignature, AActor*, DoorActor) and expose a UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable) FDoorOpenedSignature OnDoorOpened in ADoor. When the door opens you call OnDoorOpened. Broadcast(this), and all bound listeners receive the event. Bindings are commonly made with OnDoorOpened. AddDynamic(this, &ASoundEmitter::PlayDoorSound) in C++ or by using the Blueprint assign node. A key benefit is decoupling: the door doesn't know which systems care — audio, UI, analytics — they simply bind. Common pitfalls include forgetting to bind, so Broadcast has no effect, or failing to remove bindings from objects that will be destroyed, which can cause invalid calls. Unreal's object lifetime and garbage collection reduce risk for UObject-based listeners, but for safety remove dynamic bindings in EndPlay or OnDestroy if you used raw pointers. Example scenario: ADoor broadcasts OnDoorOpened and a separate UDoorWidget updates a UI counter when it hears the event. This pattern makes it easy to attach new responses to an event without editing ADoor's implementation.

keyIdea.title: Delegate pattern
keyIdea.text: Declare a dynamic multicast delegate and broadcast to notify listeners; use AddDynamic to bind handlers and RemoveDynamic to unbind as needed.

content.html:
Definition › Event Dispatchers
Declare, broadcast, bind
// ADoor.h (excerpt)
DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam(FDoorOpenedSignature, AActor*, DoorActor);

UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable, Category = "Interaction")
FDoorOpenedSignature OnDoorOpened;

// ADoor.cpp (inside Interact_Implementation)
OnDoorOpened.Broadcast(this);

// Binding from another actor
OnDoorOpened.AddDynamic(this, &ASoundEmitter::PlayDoorSound);
Best practices & gotchas
  • Use BlueprintAssignable to let designers bind in Blueprint easily.
  • RemoveDynamic or clear bindings when listeners are destroyed to avoid invalid callbacks.
  • Delegates are ideal for UI updates, audio, or telemetry that should not affect core logic flow.
  • Broadcast with minimal data to keep coupling low; pass the actor or an ID and let listeners query state if needed.
Key takeaway
Use delegates to let many systems listen and react to a single event while keeping the broadcaster agnostic of listeners.

screens.title: Interaction manager and tracing integration
screens.subtitle: Storing current interactable, highlight states, and managing multiple hits

narration.text: Your player character needs a predictable way to find and manage interactable objects each frame. The common architectural pattern is an interaction manager or component on the player that performs the visibility trace, highlights the current candidate, and stores it as a TScriptInterface reference. UpdateInteractionTrace runs the trace, checks Implements<UInteractableInterface>, and sets CurrentInteractableActor. SetObject and SetInterface accordingly. If the new actor changes from the previous frame, update highlight visuals and UI prompts. When multiple interactables are in range, choose a priority rule — distance, screen-center weight, or explicit priority tags — and pick the top candidate. A misconception is treating the trace as the interaction moment; the trace only identifies candidates. The actual state change should happen in InteractInput after verifying CanInteract. Also ensure CurrentInteractableActor is a UPROPERTY so garbage collection keeps the object alive while referenced. Example: when two doors overlap, prefer the one closer to camera center so player input acts on the object they expect. Finally, handle corner cases where Interact destroys the highlighted actor; clear CurrentInteractableActor and update the UI immediately to avoid stale references. This architecture cleanly separates detection, display, and action, improving maintainability and testing.

keyIdea.title: Architecture pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a player interaction component to trace, pick a candidate, highlight it, and store a TScriptInterface to invoke Execute_ calls on input.

content.html:
Architecture › Interaction manager
Component responsibilities
  • Perform trace each tick to detect candidates.
  • Filter results by Implements<UInteractableInterface> and priority rules.
  • Set CurrentInteractableActor as a TScriptInterface and update highlight/UI.
  • Respond to InteractInput by calling Execute_CanInteract and Execute_Interact.
Priority rule example
Choose the candidate closest to camera center, then nearest by distance if tie.
Handling multiple interactables
Keep detection separate from action. The trace suggests; InteractInput acts.
Clear stored interface immediately if the object is destroyed in Interact to avoid stale references.
Use UPROPERTY() on TScriptInterface members so garbage collection is respected.
Key takeaway
Separation of detection, presentation, and action improves predictability and designer control.

screens.title: Direct calls vs Interfaces vs Dispatchers
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right communication method

narration.text: Choosing between direct function calls, interface calls, and event dispatchers depends on ownership, coupling, and the number of listeners. Direct calls are simplest: if object A owns or tightly references object B, calling B->DoThing() is reasonable. However, direct calls create strong coupling and make reuse harder. Interfaces are ideal when you want polymorphic behavior without knowing concrete classes — a single Interact call works across doors, chests, and NPCs. Interfaces provide a clean contract and let designers implement behavior in Blueprint or C++. Event dispatchers are for one-to-many scenarios: a broadcaster announces something, and any number of listeners respond. For example, ADoor broadcasts OnDoorOpened so a sound actor, analytics system, and UI widget can all react. A misconception is assuming delegates always replace interfaces; they solve a different problem — broadcasting rather than defining a contract for a single handler. Another common error is over-using delegates for single-target interactions where a direct call or interface would be simpler. Practical rule of thumb: use direct calls for owned, single-target relationships; use interfaces for polymorphic single-target actions; use delegates for many-listener or decoupled notifications. Which rule best suits the interaction you just designed?

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Direct calls for ownership, interfaces for polymorphism, delegates for broadcasting to many listeners.

content.html:
Comparison › Communication methods
Direct Function Calls

Use when an object has a clear ownership or direct reference to the callee. Fast and explicit, but tightly coupled.

Example: Weapon component calling owner->Reload().
Interfaces (UInterface)

Define a contract that many concrete classes implement. Allows polymorphic interaction without knowing the type at compile time.

Example: Interact called on any IInteractableInterface implementer.
Event Dispatchers

Broadcast events to many listeners without the broadcaster needing to know them. Great for UI, audio, and telemetry.

Example: OnDoorOpened.Broadcast(this) notifies audio and UI systems.
Decision guide
If you need single-target polymorphism, prefer interfaces. If you need many listeners, prefer delegates. Use direct calls when both objects are tightly coupled.

screens.title: AMyCharacter: Input and binding
screens.subtitle: Bind Interact input and use TScriptInterface to execute actions

narration.text: Now we connect player input to the stored interactable. In AMyCharacter. h add a UPROPERTY TScriptInterface<IInteractableInterface> CurrentInteractableActor and a UFUNCTION void InteractInput(). In SetupPlayerInputComponent bind the action "Interact" to InteractInput. UpdateInteractionTrace should set CurrentInteractableActor. SetObject(NewHitActor) and SetInterface(Cast<IInteractableInterface>(NewHitActor)) when a valid hit occurs. In InteractInput check if CurrentInteractableActor is valid, then call Execute_CanInteract(CurrentInteractableActor. GetObject(), this). If true, call Execute_Interact(CurrentInteractableActor. GetObject(), this). A common oversight is not marking the TScriptInterface with UPROPERTY, leading to a reference not being tracked by garbage collection. Another is attempting to cast the TScriptInterface back to AActor incorrectly; use GetObject() when Execute_ requires a UObject*. Example starter snippet shows the binding and the basic guard checks. After implementing, place an ADoor in the level, set collision to block visibility, run the game, look at the door to set the current interactable, and press Interact to confirm the log message. If Execute_Interact doesn't run, verify that the actor Implements<UInteractableInterface> and that the interface functions compile with BlueprintNativeEvent. AMyCharacter: Input and binding means bind an input action to interactinput, guard with caninteract, and call execute_interact using the tscriptinterface.getobject().. In practical terms, bind interact input and use tscriptinterface to execute actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Input hookup
keyIdea.text: Bind an input action to InteractInput, guard with CanInteract, and call Execute_Interact using the TScriptInterface.GetObject().

content.html:
Code › AMyCharacter input
Header & binding
// AMyCharacter.h (excerpt)
protected:
	UPROPERTY()
	TScriptInterface<IInteractableInterface> CurrentInteractableActor;

	void InteractInput();

// AMyCharacter.cpp
void AMyCharacter::SetupPlayerInputComponent(UInputComponent* PlayerInputComponent)
{
	Super::SetupPlayerInputComponent(PlayerInputComponent);
	PlayerInputComponent->BindAction("Interact", IE_Pressed, this, &AMyCharacter::InteractInput);
}
InteractInput logic
void AMyCharacter::InteractInput()
{
	if (CurrentInteractableActor)
	{
		if (CurrentInteractableActor->Execute_CanInteract(CurrentInteractableActor.GetObject(), this))
		{
			CurrentInteractableActor->Execute_Interact(CurrentInteractableActor.GetObject(), this);
		}
		else
		{
			UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Cannot interact with %s right now."), *CurrentInteractableActor.GetObject()->GetName());
		}
	}
}
Testing checklist
Confirm Trace detects actor, CurrentInteractableActor is set, CanInteract returns true, and log appears when pressing Interact.

screens.title: Declaring and using delegates on ADoor
screens.subtitle: Declare a multicast delegate, broadcast, and bind listeners

narration.text: To let multiple systems react when ADoor opens, declare a dynamic multicast delegate in ADoor. h using DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam with an AActor* parameter for the door. Add a UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable) so Blueprints can bind. In Interact_Implementation, after toggling bIsOpen, call OnDoorOpened. Broadcast(this) to notify listeners. Any actor or widget can bind with OnDoorOpened. AddDynamic(this, &ASoundEmitter::PlayDoorSound) in C++ or with the assign event node in Blueprint. Remember lifecycle: if a listener is a UObject that will be destroyed, remove the binding in EndPlay or its destructor using RemoveDynamic to avoid dangling calls. Unreal's garbage collector helps for UObjects, but components or raw pointer listeners still need cleanup. A common mistake is forgetting to mark the delegate property BlueprintAssignable, which prevents designers from connecting events in Blueprint. Another is assuming Broadcast will create side effects in the broadcaster; keep broadcasters minimal — they should announce an event, not perform unrelated logic. Example use: when ADoor broadcasts OnDoorOpened, a separate UDoorWidget updates a counter, and an ASoundEmitter plays a sound. This separation keeps ADoor focused and makes adding or removing listeners non-invasive. Declaring and using delegates on ADoor means expose delegates as blueprintassignable, broadcast on state change, and manage bindings to avoid dangling listeners.. In practical terms, declare a multicast delegate, broadcast, and bind listeners. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Delegate lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Expose delegates as BlueprintAssignable, broadcast on state change, and manage bindings to avoid dangling listeners.

content.html:
Process › Delegates on ADoor
Declaration & broadcast
// ADoor.h
DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam(FDoorOpenedSignature, AActor*, DoorActor);

UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable, Category = "Interaction")
FDoorOpenedSignature OnDoorOpened;

// ADoor.cpp (inside Interact_Implementation)
OnDoorOpened.Broadcast(this);
Binding & cleanup
Bind in BeginPlay or when an object needs to listen, and remove binding in EndPlay or when the listener is destroyed.
// Binding example
Door->OnDoorOpened.AddDynamic(this, &ASoundEmitter::PlayDoorSound);

// Cleanup
Door->OnDoorOpened.RemoveDynamic(this, &ASoundEmitter::PlayDoorSound);
Designer tip
Mark delegates BlueprintAssignable so designers can wire responses without C++ changes.

screens.title: Starter integration and testing checklist
screens.subtitle: A minimal workflow to validate your interaction system

narration.text: This hands-on screen gives a compact starter workflow and testing checklist so you can iterate quickly. First, create InteractableInterface with BlueprintNativeEvent functions and compile. Second, implement ADoor with Interact_Implementation that toggles bIsOpen and logs a message. Third, in ADoor add DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam and a UPROPERTY BlueprintAssignable OnDoorOpened, then call Broadcast inside Interact_Implementation. Fourth, update AMyCharacter. UpdateInteractionTrace to set CurrentInteractableActor when the trace hits Implements<UInteractableInterface>. Fifth, bind Interact input and call Execute_CanInteract/Execute_Interact using CurrentInteractableActor. GetObject(). Finally, place actors in the level and run. The testing checklist: verify collision blocks visibility, watch the log message when interacting, confirm CanInteract gating works, confirm OnDoorOpened listeners receive broadcasts, and ensure no crashes when a listener is destroyed. If something fails, compile to catch signature mismatches, check that functions use _Implementation suffix, and confirm Blueprint overrides are present if used. This checklist narrows debugging steps so you can find issues quickly and keep iterating toward a robust interaction system. Starter integration and testing checklist means follow a clear create→implement→bind→test sequence and use the checklist to debug common issues like missing _implementation or absent bindings.. In practical terms, a minimal workflow to validate your interaction system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test plan
keyIdea.text: Follow a clear create→implement→bind→test sequence and use the checklist to debug common issues like missing _Implementation or absent bindings.

content.html:
Hands-on › Starter integration
Starter checklist
  1. Create InteractableInterface.h/.cpp with BlueprintNativeEvent functions and compile.

Diagnostic tips
  • Compile after adding UINTERFACE to avoid missing symbols.
  • Check for the _Implementation suffix if the function never executes.
  • Ensure TScriptInterface is UPROPERTY so GC doesn't remove the object reference.
  • Bind delegates early and remove bindings on EndPlay to avoid crashes.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Missing bindings, dangling pointers, and interface call mistakes

narration.text: As you build event-driven interaction systems, several repeating pitfalls come up. First, missing bindings: developers sometimes call Broadcast only to find no listeners were bound; verify that AddDynamic or Blueprint assignment ran before the broadcast. Second, dangling or stale bindings: if a listener is destroyed without removing its binding and the broadcaster later calls Broadcast, you may hit invalid references. RemoveDynamic in EndPlay or ensure bindings are to UObjects that participate in garbage collection. Third, forgetting the _Implementation suffix means BlueprintNativeEvent declarations have no concrete C++ implementation and Execute_ calls may not reach the intended code. Fourth, using Execute_ incorrectly by passing the interface pointer instead of the UObject* will fail; always pass CurrentInteractableActor. GetObject() as the first parameter. Fifth, treating the trace as the action moment; a trace should only identify candidates — action should run in response to explicit input after verifying CanInteract. For each pitfall, the solution is a simple guard: check Implements<UInteractableInterface>, mark TScriptInterface as UPROPERTY, call RemoveDynamic when appropriate, and validate CanInteract before Interact. These checks make your system robust and predictable during gameplay and testing.

keyIdea.title: Avoid these errors
keyIdea.text: Bind listeners, clean up bindings, use _Implementation and Execute_ correctly, and separate detection from action.

Warning › Pitfalls
Binding & lifecycle
  • Verify AddDynamic or blueprint binding occurred before Broadcast.
  • RemoveDynamic in EndPlay or before object destruction to avoid dangling calls.
  • Prefer UObject listeners to allow GC to clear stale references.
Interface call mistakes
  • Always use Execute_Function with the UObject* first parameter for BlueprintNativeEvent functions.
  • Don't forget the _Implementation suffix when defining default C++ behavior.
  • Keep detection and action separate: trace selects candidate, input triggers action.
Quick checklist
Implements check, UPROPERTY on TScriptInterface, RemoveDynamic on end, Execute_ with GetObject, verify CanInteract before Interact.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three foundational ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize three core concepts. First, UInterface is a contract: declare functions like Interact and CanInteract as BlueprintNativeEvent so both C++ and Blueprint can implement or override behavior. Second, the Execute_ helper is the correct way to call BlueprintNativeEvent functions when you have a UObject pointer; it routes the call to either C++ _Implementation or a Blueprint override. Third, TScriptInterface is the recommended container for storing interface pointers because it keeps both the UObject and interface pointer together and, when marked with UPROPERTY, participates in garbage collection. These three ideas form the minimal, safe foundation for building interaction systems that work across C++ and Blueprints. Keep them in mind as you implement and test: define contracts, call them safely, and retain references responsibly. narration.text: Finish with three practical reminders. First, event dispatchers declared with DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE let an actor broadcast to many listeners and should be exposed as BlueprintAssignable for designer flexibility. Second, always manage bindings: AddDynamic to subscribe and RemoveDynamic or clear bindings when listeners are destroyed to avoid invalid callbacks. Third, pick the communication style to match your needs: direct calls for owned relationships, interfaces for polymorphic single-target interactions, and delegates for one-to-many notifications. These rules keep systems modular, make it easy to add new interactables or listeners, and reduce the chance of runtime crashes. As you implement your lab, use these heuristics to review design choices and keep your codebase maintainable and extensible.
